## 0.9.1 (2019-04-21)

MLflow 0.9.1 is a patch release on top of 0.9.0 containing mostly bug fixes and internal improvements. We have also included a one breaking API change in preparation for additions in MLflow 1.0 and later. This release also includes significant improvements to the Search API.

Breaking changes:

# MLflow Models

An MLflow Model is a standard format for packaging machine learning models that can be used in a
variety of downstream tools---for example, real-time serving through a REST API or batch inference
on Apache Spark. The format defines a convention that lets you save a model in different "flavors"
that can be understood by different downstream tools.

## Storage Format

Each MLflow Model is a directory containing arbitrary files, together with an `MLmodel`
file in the root of the directory that can define multiple _flavors_ that the model can be viewed
in.

The **model** aspect of the MLflow Model can either be a serialized object (e.g., a pickled `scikit-learn` model)
or a Python script (or notebook, if running in Databricks) that contains the model instance that has been defined
with the <APILink fn="mlflow.models.set_model" /> API.

Flavors are the key concept that makes MLflow Models powerful: they are a convention that deployment
tools can use to understand the model, which makes it possible to write tools that work with models
from any ML library without having to integrate each tool with each library. MLflow defines
several "standard" flavors that all of its built-in deployment tools support, such as a "Python
function" flavor that describes how to run the model as a Python function. However, libraries can
also define and use other flavors. For example, MLflow's <APILink fn="mlflow.sklearn">`mlflow.sklearn`</APILink>
library allows loading models back as a scikit-learn `Pipeline` object for use in code that is aware of
scikit-learn, or as a generic Python function for use in tools that just need to apply the model
(for example, the `mlflow deployments` tool with the option `-t sagemaker` for deploying models
to Amazon SageMaker).

### MLmodel file

All of the flavors that a particular model supports are defined in its `MLmodel` file in YAML
format. For example, running `python examples/sklearn_logistic_regression/train.py` from within the

# CLAUDE.md - MLflow Frontend Development

This file provides guidance to Claude Code when working with the MLflow frontend code in this directory.

## Consistency is Critical

**IMPORTANT**: Always be consistent with the rest of the repository. This is extremely important!

Before implementing any feature:

1. Read through similar files to understand their structure and patterns
2. Do NOT invent new components if they already exist
3. Use existing patterns and conventions found in the codebase
4. Check for similar functionality that already exists

## Development Server

**IMPORTANT**: Always start the development server from the repository root for the best development experience with hot reload:

```bash
# MUST be run from the repository root
uv run dev/run_dev_server.py > /tmp/mlflow-dev-server.log 2>&1 &

# Monitor the logs (server URLs are printed there)
tail -f /tmp/mlflow-dev-server.log
```

This provides fast edit-refresh for UI development - changes to React components will automatically reload in the browser.

## Available Yarn Scripts

When running from the repository root, use this pattern:

```bash
# Example: Run any yarn command from root
pushd mlflow/server/js && yarn <command>; popd
```

Available scripts:

```bash
# Development
yarn start              # Start dev server (port 3000) with hot reload
yarn build              # Build production bundle

# Testing
yarn test               # Run Jest tests
yarn test:watch         # Run tests in watch mode
yarn test:ci            # Run tests with coverage for CI
```

Relates to #26225 and [RFC-0014 (job executor remote plugins)](https://github.com/mlflow/rfcs/blob/main/rfcs/0014-job-executor-remote-plugins/0014-job-executor-remote-plugins.md)

### What changes are proposed in this pull request?

#26225 confined custom `@scorer` code execution to the job executor process. This PR adds an **experimental `docker` job executor backend**, so that on-demand custom scorer runs can run in a hardened container instead of on the server host.

**Per-job backend dispatch.** The executor engine (`MLFLOW_SERVER_JOB_EXECUTION_ENGINE=executor`) now runs each job on the backend recorded on its job row.
- The runner starts every configured backend: `MLFLOW_JOB_DEFAULT_EXECUTOR_BACKEND`, plus `MLFLOW_JOB_CUSTOM_SCORER_EXECUTOR_BACKEND` when it is different.
- Cancel and startup recovery go to each job's own backend.
- A job whose backend is not served fails closed.
- The old submit-time rule that the two settings must be equal is removed. Instead, setting a custom scorer backend other than `local` without the executor engine now refuses to start the server, even when the default backend names the same backend, so custom scorers cannot silently run somewhere else.

**Routing.** `AbstractJobExecutor.supports_job(job_name, params)` has a default of `True`. A custom scorer job that the custom scorer backend does not support stays on the default backend, and the router logs it.

**`DockerJobExecutor`** (`mlflow/server/jobs/docker_executor.py`). Job containers have no network, so they cannot reach the server either. Data moves through bind-mounted files:
1. On the host, the job's planner fetches the traces into a read-only input mount.
2. The container runs only the scorer (`_score_traces_from_file`) and writes its result to an output mount.
3. The host treats that output as untrusted:
   - It opens the result with `O_NOFOLLOW`, rejects anything that is not a regular file, caps the read at 8 MiB (which also bounds the memory the host uses to parse it), and type-checks every field.

rows.excerpt:
<!--

-->

### Related Issues/PRs

<!-- 🚨 Choose either "Closes" (auto-close on merge) or "Relates to" (reference only). 🚨 -->

Relates to #26012, which introduced the version-matched fallback image.

### What changes are proposed in this pull request?

When the sandbox image (`MLFLOW_SANDBOX_DOCKER_IMAGE`) is not present locally, the server builds a fallback image. Since #26012, that build installs MLflow with `_pip_mlflow_install_step`. For a development build (for example `3.16.2.dev0`) without `MLFLOW_HOME`, this runs `pip install https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/archive/refs/heads/master.zip`. A tester running a server from a PR checkout hit two problems:

1. **The build failed with no explanation.** The error only said `Failed to prepare sandbox image 'mlflow-25851-bugbash:1346f3af': The command '/bin/sh -c pip install https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/archive/refs/heads/master.zip' returned a non-zero code: 1`. pip's actual error is in `BuildError.build_log`, which was dropped.
2. **Even a successful build would have run different code.** The image would contain GitHub master, not the branch the server runs, which is the version mismatch #26012 set out to prevent. `MLFLOW_HOME` avoids this, but it is a development-only setting that only MLflow's CI sets.

This PR changes the fallback build in `mlflow/server/sandbox/container.py`:

- **A development build installs from its own source.** `MLFLOW_HOME` still takes precedence for any version, as before. Without it, a development build installs from the source checkout the server runs from. A checkout is detected from the `mlflow` package's location, when its parent has a `pyproject.toml` that declares `name = "mlflow"`. Only a development build installed into site-packages still falls back to the development branch, and it now logs a warning saying so. Released versions are unchanged and still install `mlflow==<version>`.
- **Only the package is copied.** The build context gets `pyproject.toml`, `README.md`, `LICENSE.txt` and the `mlflow/` package. It skips the non-Python parts of the package (the frontend and the Java and R clients), caches, and SQLite files (`*.db`, `*.db-*`, `*.sqlite*`).
